explain.say: Picture 100 friends choosing pizza toppings. If 30 want mushroom, should mushroom get 30 of the 100 slices? That is the idea of proportional representation, or PR: seats match the share of votes. Look at the board: five steps of a PR election.

explain.say: See the first step: in many PR systems you vote for a party, a group with shared ideas. Each party gives a ranked list of candidates. South Africa, Israel and the Netherlands work like this. Would you rather pick a person or a party?

explain.say: Now look at share out seats. If a party wins 30 percent of the votes in a 100-seat parliament, it gets about 30 seats. Many countries set a minimum, like 5 percent in Germany. Quick check: what would 20 percent of votes give?

explain.say: Because seats are spread out, one party rarely gets over half. So parties team up in a coalition, which means a government made by two or more parties. Supporters call it compromise; critics say the deals take long. What do you think?

explain.say: Here are the two systems side by side. Germany and New Zealand even mix them: one vote for a local member, one for a party. Excellent thinking! Wow: after Belgium's 2010 election, forming a government took 541 days, a world record.

faq.a: A party list is a ranked list of candidates made by each party. If the party wins 10 seats, the first 10 people on its list get them. Some countries let voters move names up the list.
Seats are divided to match each party's share of votes, using a formula such as D'Hondt or Sainte-Lague. A party with 30 percent of votes gets close to 30 percent of seats.
asks: How do you work out seats in PR?

faq.a: A coalition is a government made by two or more parties working together because none has a majority alone. Germany, the Netherlands and Japan have often had coalitions.
Many do, including South Africa, Brazil, Israel, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Indonesia. Germany and New Zealand use a mixed system with local seats too.

faq.q: Is proportional representation better than first past the post?
faq.a: It depends what you value. PR gives fairer seat shares and more voices; first past the post gives a clear local member and often a single-party government. Countries choose differently.

facts: Germany has a 5% threshold: a party usually needs at least 5% of party votes to win list seats.
New Zealand switched from first past the post to a mixed proportional system in 1996.
